turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the twenty-ninth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three up top. The seven-day plan the American president refused on Saturday was back with Qatar's mediators by Monday, with edits on it.
[curious] So the no wasn't the end of it.
It was a redraft. Second — the bond selloff everybody wrote up as a long-end panic. The two-year led, by eleven basis points.
Which makes it a sentence about the Federal Reserve, not the national debt. And third?
A hundred-and-forty-fold speed-up in open-source software that nobody can use, because a maintainer got annoyed.
[laughs] Oh, that's rough. Every engineer listening just felt that.
It's the shape of the whole issue. Things that are finished, and not fired.
Built and waiting.
Built and waiting. Right. Tehran, New York, and one word that moved.
Set it up. Saturday was the rejection.
On the White House driveway. Quote: I rejected their deal. They want to open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly.
The Strait of Hormuz, reopened within seven days.
And by Monday, officials on both sides confirmed Qatar's mediators were still working — sitting separately with each side in New York, on an amended version of the same plan.
[curious] The same plan?

The terms haven't moved. Ports unblockaded, oil sanctions waived, twelve billion dollars of frozen assets released, and a ceasefire taking in Lebanon and Yemen. What we printed on Sunday is now a draft with edits on it.

He stayed in New York to receive them. And there's a detail I can't get past — he found out from a television set. Nothing has been conveyed to us, he said. It had been broadcast. It had not been delivered.
[wry] Diplomacy by press conference.
Then on Sunday he took both registers in one breath. Even if it comes to a doomsday war — and then, without a pause — we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.
What are the other desks seeing?

Al Jazeera reads the offer as dead — dead in the water, their correspondent said — with the transactional motive: kind of throwing a bone to Trump. Beijing declines the frame and names nobody at fault. Protraction of the conflict does not serve the common interests of the parties concerned.
And the consensus read is: wait. Pressure compounds, he comes back weaker.

Two Iran specialists say that's the wrong variable. Andreas Krieg grants the premise and refuses the conclusion — the danger is that he is confusing Iranian pain with Iranian willingness to capitulate. Those are not the same thing.
[thoughtful] Mm. And Bangkok, where we owe an explanation.

Last issue we printed the governor's count against the press count and refused to settle it. It's a boundary, not a contradiction. The national toll is eight, none in Bangkok, because Bangkok counts its own — and there are three. So the honest sentence is at least eleven dead in Thailand, and at least eight in Myanmar.
Money. This is where you get pedantic and I enjoy it.
[deadpan] I live for it. Monday was a selloff, and everybody wrote it up as a term-premium shock.
And it wasn't.
Read the Treasury's own par curve column by column. The two-year rose eleven basis points. The seven-year rose nine. The ten-year, seven. The twenty-year, six.
So the front end led.
And the two-to-ten spread narrowed from thirty-six basis points to thirty-two. A flattening is a statement about the central bank, not the national debt.
A long end that leads means worry about supply and the far future. A front end that leads means the next few meetings.

The range went to three and three-quarters to four per cent on the sixteenth, twelve votes to nil. Then Saturday's rejection removed the only near-term route to cheaper crude. That's an inflation problem, and inflation prices at the front.
[curious] But everything fell. Equities, bonds, gold, bitcoin. Isn't that panic?
That's the tell, and it's the opposite. In a genuine flight to safety, gold does not do that — and gold broke through four thousand two hundred dollars to a seven-week low.
So one force is setting all four prices.
The expected path of policy, rather than the growth outlook. Not advice — and every one of those readings turns on a number that hasn't printed yet.
Which prints when?
Tomorrow. One economist reads the producer-price detail as implying core inflation too soft to justify another hike. Monday's conviction has a day of life in it.
[pause] Home. Week five of the haze.

And the story is a gap, not a reading. The plan announced on the fourth of September is real and specific — purifiers in every classroom, enclosed exam rooms when the air is Unhealthy, coolers in hospitals and nursing homes.

But school operations and exam schedules are unchanged, and the community centres open as haze refuges only above two hundred. Unhealthy starts at a hundred and one, and we've been nowhere near two hundred.
So the public refuge opens at twice the worst of it.
And the only thing cancelled so far was cancelled by a private organiser. At three in the morning on Sunday, two hours before the gun, they shortened a half-marathon to ten kilometres.
[gasps] Three in the morning.
Awards scrapped, every category non-competitive, so there are no results. And two entrants said they were offered neither refund nor compensation.
So the anger went to the money, not the call.

Runners broadly said the call itself was responsible. Which leaves the question — is Unhealthy a trigger, or a notification? And purifiers are an indoor answer: they do nothing for the outdoor workforce, where the language is advise rather than require.
Silicon. AMD bought a two-year-old lab.

About eight point two billion dollars, in its own stock, for World Labs. Fei-Fei Li becomes AMD's executive vice-president and chief scientist. And the calendar is the story — twenty-five days ago Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for just under thirteen billion.
[gasps] Twenty-five days.

Both signed. Neither closed. The open-model commons now sits inside two chip vendors' balance sheets. And Su's reason is narrower than the press release — building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires understanding how models are evolving.
[thoughtful] So the chip designer is buying a telescope pointed at its own roadmap.
That's exactly it.
What did engineers make of the price?
Hacker News asked the obvious thing — is a two-year-old company worth eight billion dollars — and answered it without flattery. These are public bets, not valuations based on product economics.
[skeptical] And there's no product commitment anywhere.

Two shipping products, named in World Labs' own post with no roadmap, and AMD's release doesn't mention them. So the test is simple. If they're fenced behind AMD's own stack within two quarters, the openness was marketing.
Now the speed-up.

On Friday a developer published optimisations to the speculative drafter inside the engine a lot of people run models on at home. Reads by reference instead of copies gave up to twenty-five times faster drafting. A sorted vector doubled it. Then Daniel Lemire joined in, and it reached a hundred and forty.
[excited] A hundred and forty. And none of it is upstream?
A maintainer got tagged by accident — on the developer's own fork, not the main repository — and replied: blocked for making me waste my time. Yesterday the thread was locked to collaborators.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.

And here's the honest half. This is a speed-up on the drafter, not on inference. A forward pass is measured in milliseconds; the saving is about a hundred and sixty-four microseconds per drafted token.
So what does it do for tokens per second?
Somebody asked exactly that. In a thread that got to eighty-three points, nobody answered. Until there's an end-to-end benchmark, it's beautiful work of unquantified benefit.
And the pull request we've been watching got its first approving review on Sunday. The repository requires two.
One of two.
One of two. That's the week's delta.
Built and waiting. Headphones.

The Sonos Ace Ultra goes on general sale here today at six hundred and ninety-nine dollars. New drivers, ten microphones against eight, up to thirty-five hours with cancelling on. And the feature that justifies the premium shipped in early access.
[scoffs] On sale day.

These are the company's own stated limitations. Lossless and spatial audio aren't supported over the link, so it's compressed stereo. It needs Wi-Fi, so it fails the moment you leave the house. And your speaker grouping dissolves when audio links to it.
Anything genuinely buy-once about it?

Two things, and they're real. The cushions are user-replaceable for thirty-nine US dollars, and so is the battery, for twenty-five. In a category that treats a dead cell as the end of the product, that's the buy-once argument in parts.
Which is the desk that exists for that exact question.

The Atelier, and it's dress shirts — where the cloth label is the least reliable thing on the garment. Start with the number everyone misreads. A hundred and twenty s is not threads per inch. It's the fineness of the yarn.
So a two-hundred single-ply —

Is thinner and weaker, not better. Above about a hundred, the number implies two yarns twisted together. One New York shirtmaker describes the fashionable compact single-plies as, quote, thin and slimey.
[laughs] From a man with every reason to sell you the dearer cloth.

Which is what makes it a ceiling worth trusting. Now the labels. One famous English mill name, founded in seventeen ninety-six, has been Italian-owned since nineteen ninety-two — and its owner's own page lists weaving in Egypt, spinning in Hungary.

And one company near Como sells shirting under thirteen house names, including a Swiss one that still calls itself a historical Swiss company. The trade's verdict is unsentimental. It is just a name. Nothing woven in Switzerland.
So what do I actually do in the shop?

Two tests, and they cost nothing. Count the stitches on the cuff — eighteen to the inch is the floor, the best houses state twenty-two. Then pinch the collar leaf: a fused collar moves as one board, an unfused one shifts.
[excited] The whole desk in two gestures. And for our weather?

None of this literature is written for us — it's written for English summers. At thirty degrees and eighty per cent humidity, evaporation is throttled, so the job is airflow, not wicking. Which means voile — and the catch is that you can see through it. Hence twill, for most people.
[excited] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week.
Every week. Orienteering.

The premise is almost embarrassingly simple. You're given a map and a list of control points, and you visit them in order, as fast as you can, through terrain you have never seen. A compass is allowed. Satellite navigation is not. Get one wrong and you're disqualified — no appeal.
At what scale do people do this?
Two days from now, ninety-eight teams start a five-day race across Corsica with no satellite navigation at all. They're handed the maps at the line.
[gasps] That's a film.

What makes it a sport rather than a walk is that the straight line is almost never the right answer. The map prints a red line between controls, and the whole game is choosing which of the wrong routes around it is least wrong.
And there's a vocabulary for that.

A beautiful one. You pick an attackpoint — a large unmistakable feature near the control — run to that confidently, then navigate precisely. You aim off to one side of a control on a stream, so when you hit it you know which way to turn. And you keep a catching feature beyond it, so you know when you've overrun.
[warmly] Oh, that's lovely. How old is this?
Eighteen ninety-seven, in Norway. And the map is a specification, not a drawing. Colour is a claim about how fast you can run. Yellow is open land. White is forest you can run through.
[curious] Wait. White is runnable forest?
A newcomer's first shock is that white does not mean empty. Darker greens mean thicker undergrowth.
[laughs] I'd have had that exactly backwards. Is there a scene here?
Small and real. A league, a national race, urban wayfinder events, one on Pulau Ubin. What we don't have is Nordic forest. What we do have is sprint terrain.

The sceptics here are the recruiters themselves. One noted that Florida alone puts two and a half thousand school-age people through events every year — then asked what nobody has answered. Then they stop. Why do they stop?

Another was blunter: the sport only works for a small, rare type of participant. And the diagnosis — culture wants low-commitment outdoor activity. A sport needing a club, a map, a start time and a forest is not that.
Gear. Which is where you get interesting.
The timing card is the first real purchase, and it just became compulsory. The main vendor discontinued its two old cards after twenty-seven years, which killed the borrowed-card economy at a stroke.
The Norwegian rival went harder. Every tag below a certain serial has to be replaced, because the batteries are cast in.
[scoffs] So both vendors, inside eighteen months, obsoleted the hardware their own communities already owned.

That's the sentence. Then the compass, and the mistake a Singapore buyer makes. Compasses are balanced for a magnetic zone, because the field dips at a different angle by latitude. The wrong one tilts and drags.
So buy the global-balanced one.
About seventy-two euros — and a New Zealand race legislates it outright.
And the shoes. This is my favourite part.

They're studded, and the best-regarded ones do not last. The verdict on one race flagship, from the man who wrote the mapping software half this sport runs on: it is expensive and will not last more than fifty kilometres.
[gasps] Fifty kilometres? At what price?
About two hundred euros.
That's a consumable.

And for a buy-once reader the logic inverts. Here the premium buys lightness, and lightness costs life. The durable middle is about a hundred and forty euros — and costs more direct from the maker than from the specialists.
What's the hidden craft?

Mapping, and the economics are brutal. British guidance puts field survey at sixteen to sixty hours per square kilometre — four square kilometres could take sixteen months for a volunteer with ten free hours a month.
[exhales] Sixteen months. Didn't laser scanning fix that?

That was my question, and the answer is no. A free Finnish engine turns airborne laser data into a usable basemap, and plenty of mappers prefer its contours. But its own author volunteers the limit — it does badly with thin laser data.
The laser makes the basemap. It does not touch the fieldwork — and the most honest verdict came from a beginner: I used the laser data to produce contours, and heavily edited them by hand.
Ninety days. What do I actually do?

Spend a fortnight spending nothing — read the analysis site, watch other people's routes, turn up to an event in borrowed shoes. Then buy in order: compass first, the cheapest permanent upgrade in the sport, then your own card. Shoes last, and buy the durable model. About three hundred and thirty euros all in, and the return fare from Changi is the rest.
Culture, fast, because the top of the American box office is absurd.
The number-one film in America last weekend was Avengers: Endgame. Released in April, twenty nineteen.
[laughs] Seven years old.
Re-cut with added scenes from the next film, it took twenty-six million dollars from three thousand screens — and beat three new wide releases that all reviewed well.
And it's being credited to the old film's total?

Which is the records-table artefact worth naming. That money goes onto the twenty-nineteen film's cumulative rather than being tracked separately, and that's what generates the headline about the all-time record.
Against a record-holder that has itself been re-released repeatedly to defend the same crown. Disney isn't selling a film. It's selling a trailer with a film attached.
Family desk.

Somebody finally asked teenagers which app it happened on. Four hundred and seventy-two American adolescents, twenty platforms. On feeling worse about yourself — Instagram sixteen point six per cent, TikTok thirteen point four, YouTube four point one.
[gasps] Four to one.

And on sleep, TikTok forty-two per cent against text messaging at ten. A difference a parent can act on — and exactly the kind a self-report survey is worst at measuring. There are no odds ratios anywhere in it, so anyone printing X times more likely has invented it.
And the bigger study?

Forty thousand Swedish adolescents at eleven, thirteen and fifteen. Problematic social-media use was most strongly associated with trouble falling asleep at eleven — and the association was weaker in the older ones, not stronger.
[thoughtful] That's the opposite of what every parent assumes.

It's the opposite of what I assumed. Put it beside the local policy — school devices now lock by default at half past ten. The curfew is doing the one thing the largest study supports, and it matters most for the youngest child in the house.
General guidance, not medical advice.

Correct. And fitness, quickly, because it changed my week. A hundred thousand wrist accelerometers say the variable isn't ten thousand steps — it's your peak cadence, the average over your thirty highest-stepping minutes of the day. Risk bottoms out near a hundred steps a minute, three steps every two seconds, and above ten thousand it flattens. The catch is that no mainstream wearable shows you that number. Not medical advice.
[pause] The Undercurrent.
Taiwan. Twenty-three million people supplying about a fifth of one social network's traffic on earth. More than the United States.
Which network?
Threads. Except Taiwanese people don't call it that. They call it cui — a character meaning crisp, crunchy, brittle. And of a person, fragile.
[curious] Why that word?
Mandarin has no th sound, so users needed something sayable, and that was the rough phonetic stab that won. Now users are crisp friends, and the feed is the river channel.
And nobody designed this. The platform launched in twenty twenty-three and was abandoned within weeks. Taiwanese adoption began that November and accelerated through the presidential election.
[thoughtful] So a network built expressly to avoid politics became, in one country, the place politics happens.

And its own product head named Taiwan as central to its success, and named elections as the reason. What Taiwan built is a public square nobody built — privately owned, foreign, publishing no per-country numbers, answerable to no Taiwanese regulator.
And the bill for that arrived.

Three times in six months. April was an arithmetic error — a claim that Taiwan held ninety-four million accounts, four times its population. Somebody had multiplied a global user count by Taiwan's share of web traffic.
[sighs] And it travelled because people wanted it to be true.

Which sets the standard for everything after. June was an accident in California — an age-verification mechanism began suspending accounts as under-thirteens. Within two days the casualty list included a legislator, a former Taipei mayor, and overnight the foreign ministry's own account.
What could the government actually do?
Ask. Roughly ninety per cent were back within three days.
[pause] Which means ten per cent were not.
And no statute compels an offshore platform to verify accounts or disclose anything. In the week its own foreign ministry vanished, the state's only instrument was a press release asking nicely.
And the third instalment is the new one.

A content farm in Hebei running more than twelve hundred domains. Against Taiwan it ran five hundred and forty-nine inauthentic accounts, producing at least four hundred and sixty-seven thousand posts.
That sounds like an influence operation.

Here's the uncomfortable part. Nought point three eight per cent of them were political — and that content was ideologically mixed, not hostile to any one party. Eighty-three per cent carried a link back to a farm domain.

So it isn't propaganda — it's programmatic advertising. It's a business. And the method is patient in a way propaganda rarely is. Register domains in bulk, fill them with stolen copy, create accounts with stolen profile photographs.

And then they raise the account — feeding it entertainment news and life hacks for weeks until the algorithm and the reader both file it as ordinary. Only then attach the link, keeping politics to a trickle so it never trips the heuristics.
And five hundred and sixty-six genuine Taiwanese users shared those domains of their own accord — at which point it's inside the authentic graph.
And then June.
A separate investigator, looking at something else entirely, documented two hundred and ninety-four coordinated accounts launched in May, presenting as women seeking Taiwanese men.
How coordinated?
A hundred and eighteen share a handle pattern. Seventy posted identical profile text. Active nine in the morning to seven at night Beijing time, with a break between twelve and one.
[gasps] A lunch break.
The profiles say currently in Taiwan. Most that disclose are in China. And as of the date of the analysis, the number of political posts across all two hundred and ninety-four accounts was —
[whispers] Don't say zero.

Zero. They're pre-positioned. And the researcher supplies the timetable: fake accounts usually start emerging roughly six months before an election. May plus six is November, and Taiwan votes island-wide on the twenty-eighth of November.
[exhales] So what's the correct frame?

Not China is flooding Taiwan with propaganda. On the published evidence, it isn't. What's been built over thirty-one months is rentable distribution inside the platform where Taiwan argues with itself.
[thoughtful] Which is worse.

Worse, because an ad-arbitrage business has no ideology to abandon and no reason to refuse a better offer. And the strongest sceptic is the lab that wrote the report — reading this as an election attack reads past a finding of nought point three eight per cent.
So what do we watch?

Whether that political share moves. Whether the digital ministry converts June's embarrassment into a statute rather than a press release. And whether a text feed can originate a political brand faster than a party can.
Meaning the mayoral race.
The governing party's Taipei candidate passed six hundred and forty thousand followers yesterday. The sitting mayor, who actually holds the city, has eighty-eight thousand.
And the challenger's own slogan wasn't devised by the campaign. Supporters made orange placards at a night market in August while he canvassed, and the campaign adopted it within weeks.
[warmly] That's the good half of this story.
Taiwan chose this square partly because it felt clean. It will vote in it in November knowing it is not. That's not a worse position. It's an honest one, and more than most democracies can say.
[pause] The guns exist. They're pointed at a slimming advertisement.
And nobody has decided what to do with them.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
